etymology: Hebrew Yokeved, "the LORD is glory"; the mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, who hid the infant Moses by faith.
biblical_def: Jochebed was the wife of Amram, of the tribe of Levi, and the mother of three of the greatest figures of the Old Testament: Aaron the high priest, Miriam the prophetess, and Moses the deliverer (Exo 6:20). She is remembered above all for the courageous faith by which she preserved the infant Moses. When Pharaoh decreed that every Hebrew son be cast into the Nile, Jochebed hid her child for three months, and when she could hide him no longer, she made an ark of bulrushes, daubed it with pitch, and laid the baby among the reeds by the river's brink — entrusting him to the providence of God. Pharaoh's own daughter found him, and by Miriam's quick wit Jochebed was hired to nurse her own son, raising him in the knowledge of his people before he entered Pharaoh's house. The Epistle to the Hebrews enrolls her faith among the heroes: "By faith Moses, when he was born, was hid three months of his parents, because they saw he was a proper child; and they were not afraid of the king's commandment" (Heb 11:23). Jochebed stands in the dictionary as the faithful mother who defied a murderous decree to preserve her child, a witness to the power of a godly mother's faith and to the providence of God that turns a tyrant's death-edict into the saving of a deliverer.
webster_summary: Mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam (Exo 6:20); who by faith hid the infant Moses against Pharaoh's death-decree (Heb 11:23), a witness to a godly mother's courage and God's providence.

corruption_summary: Jochebed's faith honors the recovery of godly courage to defy a murderous decree and of the high calling of mothers, against a fear of man that yields to wicked law and a culture that despises the sanctity of infant life.
corruption_paragraphs: Fear-of-man correction. Pharaoh commanded the death of the Hebrew sons, but Jochebed and Amram "were not afraid of the king's commandment" (Heb 11:23). The dictionary holds that an unjust decree against innocent life does not bind the conscience; the godly fear God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and a wicked law commanding the destruction of children is to be resisted, not obeyed. Jochebed's faith defied the tyrant to preserve the life God had given.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the high and holy calling of motherhood. Jochebed's faith, courage, and early nurture of Moses shaped the deliverer of Israel before ever he entered Pharaoh's court. The dictionary commends the honor of godly mothers: the hand that rocks the cradle and teaches the child the fear of the LORD does a work of eternal weight, and the faith of a mother may, under God, preserve and form a servant who changes the course of nations.

etymology: The two Hebrew midwives who feared God and refused Pharaoh's command to kill the male infants (Exo 1:15-21).
biblical_def: Shiphrah and Puah were two Hebrew midwives whom Pharaoh commanded to kill every male child born to the Hebrew women, that Israel's growth might be checked. "But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive" (Exo 1:17). When Pharaoh demanded why, they answered that the Hebrew women were vigorous and delivered before the midwives came. For their courageous defiance of a murderous decree, "God dealt well with the midwives... And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that he made them houses" (Exo 1:20-21) — that is, He blessed them with families of their own. Their fear of God outweighed their fear of the most powerful man on earth, and they chose to protect innocent life at great personal risk rather than obey an evil law. Shiphrah and Puah stand in the dictionary as the God-fearing midwives who would not shed innocent blood, a lasting witness that the fear of God must govern obedience to human authority, that an unjust command to destroy the innocent is not to be obeyed, and that God remembers and rewards those who protect life and defy wickedness for His sake.
webster_summary: Two Hebrew midwives (Exo 1:15-21) who feared God and refused Pharaoh's command to kill the male infants, saving the children alive; God dealt well with them and made them houses.

corruption_summary: Shiphrah and Puah honor the recovery of the fear of God above the fear of man and of righteous refusal to obey an unjust command, against a servility that complies with evil law and a contempt for the sanctity of life.
corruption_paragraphs: Unjust-law-obeyed correction. Some teach that the believer must always obey the civil authority, even when it commands sin. Shiphrah and Puah feared God and disobeyed a direct royal command to murder, and God commended and rewarded them. The dictionary holds that human authority is to be honored within its bounds, but a command to do evil — especially to shed innocent blood — is not to be obeyed; we ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and the fear of God governs all lesser allegiances.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the protection of innocent life as a fear-of-God duty. The midwives risked their lives to save defenseless infants. The dictionary commends their example with abiding application: the lives of the unborn and the newborn are precious to God, and those who fear Him will protect rather than destroy them, even against the decrees of the powerful. God remembers such faithfulness, and dealt well with the midwives who would not kill.

etymology: Hebrew Qeturah, "incense"; the wife Abraham took after Sarah's death, mother of six sons.
biblical_def: Keturah was the wife (also called a concubine) whom Abraham took after the death of Sarah, by whom he had six more sons: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah (Gen 25:1-2; 1 Chr 1:32). From these descended various Arabian peoples, most notably the Midianites through Midian. Yet Scripture is careful to mark the distinction of the covenant line: "Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac. But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country" (Gen 25:5-6). The sons of Keturah were blessed with gifts and a place, but the covenant promise and inheritance passed through Isaac, the son of promise, alone. Keturah's many sons fulfilled in part God's word that Abraham would be a father of many nations, even as the line of redemption ran through the one chosen seed. Keturah stands in the dictionary as Abraham's later wife and the mother of many peoples, a witness both to the breadth of God's promise that Abraham should father many nations, and to the particularity of the covenant, which passed not to all his sons but to Isaac, the child of promise, through whom the blessing of all nations would finally come in Christ.
webster_summary: Abraham's wife after Sarah's death (Gen 25:1-2), mother of six sons including Midian; her sons received gifts but the covenant inheritance passed to Isaac alone, marking the particularity of the promise.

corruption_summary: Keturah's account honors the recovery of the particularity of the covenant alongside the breadth of God's promise, against a universalism that erases the distinction of the chosen line of redemption.
corruption_paragraphs: Covenant-flattened correction. It might seem that all Abraham's sons should share alike in the promise; Scripture marks a clear distinction: Isaac received the inheritance, the others gifts. The dictionary holds the particularity of the covenant: God's redemptive line ran not through every descendant but through the chosen seed, Isaac, and then Jacob, narrowing to the one Seed, Christ. The breadth of God's mercy to the nations does not erase the particular line through which redemption came.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the harmony of God's universal promise and His particular election. Abraham was made "a father of many nations" (Gen 17:5), fulfilled in part through Keturah's many sons; yet the covenant blessing came through Isaac alone. The dictionary commends both truths: God's purpose embraces all nations, and accomplishes it through a particular, chosen line, until in Christ the blessing of Abraham reaches every family of the earth.

etymology: Hebrew Dinah, "judgment" or "vindicated"; the daughter of Jacob and Leah, defiled at Shechem.
biblical_def: Dinah was the daughter of Jacob and Leah, whose defilement set off one of the darkest episodes in the patriarchal narratives. "And Dinah the daughter of Leah, which she bare unto Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the land" (Gen 34:1); and Shechem, a Hivite prince, "saw her, he took her, and lay with her, and defiled her." Though Shechem then desired to marry her and his father sought a covenant of intermarriage, Dinah's brothers Simeon and Levi, enraged at the violation of their sister, deceitfully proposed that the men of the city be circumcised, and then, while the men lay sore, fell on the city and slew all the males, plundering it and taking the women and children. Jacob rebuked their cruelty and treachery, fearing the surrounding peoples, and on his deathbed he pronounced a curse upon their fierce anger (Gen 49:5-7). The whole account is told without approval of any party's sin — neither Shechem's violation, nor the brothers' murderous revenge. Dinah stands in the dictionary as the daughter whose defilement brought sorrow and bloodshed, a sober witness to the dangers that attend a careless venturing into the world, to the wickedness of those who violate the vulnerable, and to the destructive excess of vengeance that takes justice into its own cruel hands.
webster_summary: The daughter of Jacob and Leah (Gen 34), defiled by Shechem; her brothers Simeon and Levi avenged her by deceit and massacre, which Jacob rebuked and later cursed; a sober account of violation and vengeful excess.

corruption_summary: Dinah's account is corrupted when it is read to excuse either the violation she suffered or the murderous revenge it provoked; Scripture condemns both the predator and the vengeful excess.
corruption_paragraphs: Violation-excused correction. A culture that minimizes sexual sin might soften Shechem's crime; Scripture names it defilement, a grievous wrong against a vulnerable young woman. The dictionary holds the seriousness of such violation and the worth of those it harms; God's law surrounds the vulnerable with protection, and the predator who takes advantage of the defenseless stands condemned before the holy God who sees and avenges.

This entry faces little further postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the condemnation of vengeful excess. Simeon and Levi's response — deceit, mass murder, and plunder — was not justice but cruelty, and Jacob cursed their fierce anger (Gen 49:7). The dictionary commends the balance: real wrong calls for real justice, but vengeance that takes the sword into its own hand, slaughtering the innocent with the guilty, is itself condemned. "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19), and Dinah's story warns against the cruelty that masquerades as the defense of the wronged.

etymology: Hebrew Zilpah; Leah's handmaid, given to Jacob as a wife, mother of Gad and Asher.
biblical_def: Zilpah was the handmaid whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah, and whom Leah in turn gave to Jacob as a wife when she had left off bearing, in the rivalry between the sisters for children. Zilpah bore Jacob two sons: Gad, whose name Leah linked to a troop coming, and Asher, "happy" (Gen 30:9-13). From these two sons descended the tribes of Gad and Asher, full members of the twelve tribes of Israel, inheriting their portions in the promised land. The arrangement reflects the disordered household that resulted from Jacob's polygamy — two wives and two concubines competing for honor and offspring, a tangle of jealousy and strife that Scripture records without approval, showing the bitter fruit of departing from God's design of one man and one wife. Yet God in His sovereignty wove even these broken family circumstances into the building of His covenant nation, raising up two of the tribes of Israel through Zilpah's sons. Zilpah stands in the dictionary as a mother of two tribes of Israel, a witness both to the disorder and sorrow that flow from polygamy and rivalry, and to the overruling providence of God, who built the twelve tribes of His people even through the troubled households of the patriarchs.
webster_summary: Leah's handmaid given to Jacob as a wife (Gen 30:9-13), mother of Gad and Asher; a witness to the disorder of polygamy and to God's providence in building the tribes of Israel even through it.

corruption_paragraphs: Polygamy-normalized correction. The patriarchal households, with their multiple wives and concubines, are recorded in Scripture but never commended; they are marked by jealousy, rivalry, and sorrow. The dictionary holds God's design from the beginning: one man and one wife, joined as one flesh (Gen 2:24). The strife in Jacob's house — Leah and Rachel contending, handmaids given as wives — is the bitter fruit of departing from that design, a warning rather than a pattern.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God's sovereign overruling of broken circumstances. Out of Jacob's tangled and rivalrous household, God built the twelve tribes of Israel, two of them through Zilpah's sons Gad and Asher. The dictionary commends this comfort: the Lord is not defeated by the disorder and sin of human families, but weaves even troubled and irregular circumstances into the accomplishment of His covenant purposes, raising up His people and His Christ through histories marked by human failure.

etymology: Hebrew Bilhah; Rachel's handmaid, given to Jacob as a wife, mother of Dan and Naphtali.
biblical_def: Bilhah was the handmaid whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel, and whom Rachel, in her grief at being childless, gave to Jacob as a wife, saying, "Behold my maid Bilhah, go in unto her; and she shall bear upon my knees, that I may also have children by her" (Gen 30:3). Bilhah bore Jacob two sons: Dan, in whose name Rachel said, "God hath judged me," and Naphtali, "my wrestling" (Gen 30:5-8). From these descended the tribes of Dan and Naphtali. Bilhah appears again in a darker note: after Rachel's death, "Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine: and Israel heard it" (Gen 35:22) — a grievous sin for which Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, forfeited the dignity of his birthright, as Jacob declared on his deathbed (Gen 49:3-4). Bilhah thus stands at the center of both the building of Israel and one of its early disgraces. She stands in the dictionary as the mother of two tribes of Israel and the occasion of Reuben's fall, a witness to the disorder that flowed from the patriarchs' polygamy, to the lasting consequences of sin against the family, and to the providence of God that built His covenant nation even through such troubled and broken households.
webster_summary: Rachel's handmaid given to Jacob as a wife (Gen 30:3-8), mother of Dan and Naphtali; later the occasion of Reuben's sin (Gen 35:22), which cost him his birthright; a witness to family disorder and its consequences.

corruption_summary: Bilhah's account honors the recovery of God's design of marriage and the lasting consequences of sin against the family, against a normalizing of polygamy and a making-light of grievous sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Consequence-denied correction. Reuben's sin with Bilhah might seem a minor lapse, soon forgotten; Scripture shows otherwise. It cost Jacob's firstborn the pre-eminence of his birthright, and Jacob recalled it with grief decades later on his deathbed (Gen 49:4). The dictionary holds that sin, especially sin that defiles the family, bears lasting consequence; what is done in a moment may forfeit blessings and dignities for a lifetime, and the God who sees does not overlook the dishonoring of His order.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is again God's design of marriage against the disorder of the patriarchal household, and His providence over it. From Bilhah's sons came two tribes of Israel; through a household marked by rivalry and sin, God still built His covenant people. The dictionary commends both the warning and the comfort: human families fail and sin grievously, yet the Lord, who hates the sin, sovereignly accomplishes His redemptive purposes even through broken and dishonored histories.

etymology: Hebrew Ritspah, "hot coal"; the concubine of Saul whose vigil over her slain sons moved King David.
biblical_def: Rizpah was a concubine of King Saul, the daughter of Aiah, remembered for a vigil of extraordinary devotion and grief. In the days of David, a three-year famine came because of Saul's broken oath and bloodshed against the Gibeonites; to make atonement, seven of Saul's descendants, including Rizpah's two sons, were given to the Gibeonites and hanged. "And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night" (2 Sam 21:10). For months this mother kept watch over the exposed bodies of the slain, driving off the scavengers, refusing to let her dead be dishonored. When David was told of Rizpah's faithful vigil, he was moved to gather the bones of Saul and Jonathan and of the hanged men, and gave them honorable burial in the family tomb; "and after that God was intreated for the land" (2 Sam 21:14). Rizpah stands in the dictionary as the grieving mother of the long vigil, a witness to the depth of a mother's love and loyalty, to the honor owed even to the dead, and to the tender response of a king moved by her faithfulness to do right by the fallen.
webster_summary: A concubine of Saul (2 Sam 21:8-14) whose months-long vigil guarded the bodies of her slain sons from the birds and beasts; her devotion moved David to give the dead honorable burial.

corruption_summary: Rizpah needs no defense from redefinition; her vigil witnesses to the depth of a mother's love, the honor owed to the dead, and the tender response of a king moved by faithful devotion.
corruption_paragraphs: Devotion-diminished correction. A hurried, self-protective age has little patience for the costly, lingering love Rizpah showed, keeping a months-long watch over the dead. The dictionary holds the worth of such faithful devotion: love that does not abandon its own even in death, that bears long grief and discomfort for the sake of honoring the fallen, reflects something of the steadfast love of God, who does not forget His own even in the grave.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honor owed to the dead and the response of compassion to faithful grief. Rizpah's vigil moved King David to gather and bury the bones of the slain with honor. The dictionary commends both: the bodies of the dead are to be treated with dignity, not contempt; and the godly, like David, are moved by the faithful love of the grieving to do right by the fallen, weeping with them that weep (Rom 12:15).
roots_summary: A concubine of Saul (2 Sam 21:8-14) whose months-long vigil guarded the bodies of her slain sons; her devotion moved David to give the dead honorable burial.

etymology: Greek Hanna, from Hebrew Hannah, "grace"; the aged widow and prophetess who saw the infant Christ in the temple.
biblical_def: Anna was a prophetess of great age who saw and gave thanks for the infant Christ when He was brought to the temple, one of the two devout elders (with Simeon) who recognized the Messiah at His presentation. Luke records that she was "of a great age, and had lived with an husband seven years from her virginity; and she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day" (Luke 2:36-37). When Joseph and Mary brought Jesus to present Him to the Lord, Anna "coming in that instant gave thanks likewise unto the Lord, and spake of him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem" (Luke 2:38). For decades she had given herself to worship, fasting, and prayer in the temple, and God honored her long faithfulness with the sight of His salvation in the flesh, and made her a herald of the Redeemer to all who awaited Him. Anna stands in the dictionary as the faithful aged widow who saw the Christ, a witness to the honor God puts upon a long life of worship and prayer, to the spiritual fruitfulness of godly widowhood, and to the joy of recognizing and proclaiming the Redeemer when He comes.
webster_summary: An aged widow and prophetess (Luke 2:36-38) who served God night and day in the temple with fasting and prayer, and who saw the infant Christ at His presentation and spoke of Him to all who awaited redemption.

corruption_summary: Anna honors the recovery of the dignity and fruitfulness of godly widowhood and aged saints, and of a life of worship and prayer, against a culture that despises the old and discounts the hidden ministry of prayer.
corruption_paragraphs: Age-despised correction. A youth-obsessed culture discounts the aged as past usefulness. Anna, at eighty-four, was at the height of her usefulness, given the honor of seeing and proclaiming the Christ after a lifetime of worship. The dictionary holds the dignity of aged saints: those who have served God long are not cast aside but honored, and the hoary head found in the way of righteousness is a crown of glory (Prov 16:31); the old who walk with God are among His most fruitful servants.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the fruitfulness of a life of worship and prayer. Anna departed not from the temple, serving God night and day, the very picture of the widow indeed who trusts in God and continues in supplications (1 Tim 5:5). The dictionary commends this hidden ministry: the prayers and worship of faithful saints, especially godly widows, are a great and often unseen labor, dear to God, and Anna's long vigil of prayer was crowned with the sight of the world's Redeemer.

etymology: Greek Phoibe, "bright, radiant"; a servant of the church at Cenchrea, commended by Paul, likely the bearer of the Epistle to the Romans.
biblical_def: Phebe was a Christian woman of the church at Cenchrea, the eastern port of Corinth, whom the apostle Paul commended in the closing chapter of his Epistle to the Romans, and who is widely believed to have carried that letter to Rome. "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea: that ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also" (Rom 16:1-2). The word translated "servant" (Greek diakonos) marks her as one who ministered in the practical service of the church, and "succourer" (a patroness or helper) shows she had given generous aid to many believers and to Paul himself. Paul honored her by name, asked the Roman church to receive and assist her, and entrusted to her, it seems, the most weighty doctrinal letter of the New Testament. Phebe stands in the dictionary as a faithful servant and helper of the church, a witness to the honored and vital ministry of godly women in the service, hospitality, and support of the saints, exercised within the good order God has appointed, and a model of the practical love that succours many for Christ's sake.
webster_summary: A servant (diakonos) and "succourer" of the church at Cenchrea (Rom 16:1-2), commended by Paul and likely the bearer of the Epistle to the Romans; a model of the honored ministry of godly women in serving and aiding the saints.

Called a "servant" (diakonos) and a "succourer of many" (Rom 16:2).
Likely the bearer of the Epistle to the Romans.
A model of women's honored service and support of the saints.

Titus 2:3

corruption_summary: Phebe honors the recovery of the honored, vital ministry of godly women within biblical order, against both a feminism that demands the offices Scripture reserves and a neglect that overlooks the indispensable service of women in the church.
corruption_paragraphs: Women's-ministry-neglected correction. Some so guard the church's order that they overlook the rich and honored ministries Scripture gives to women. Paul commended Phebe by name, called her a servant and succourer of many, and entrusted her with his greatest letter. The dictionary holds that godly women have vital, honored ministries — hospitality, mercy, service, the support of gospel work, the teaching of younger women (Titus 2:3-5) — and that the church which fails to recognize and value such service is poorer for it.

This entry faces a real postmodern pressure. Some press Phebe's title diakonos to overturn the biblical reservation of the teaching and ruling offices of the church to qualified men. The dictionary holds the complementarian order of Scripture: women serve in countless honored ways, as Phebe did, but the offices of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church are entrusted to men (1 Tim 2:12; 3:1-7). To honor Phebe rightly is to honor both her real and commended ministry and the good order within which she served, refusing to set her example against the Word that records it.

etymology: A dynastic title (not a personal name) of the queens of the Ethiopians (Cush), whose treasurer was converted under Philip (Acts 8:27).
biblical_def: Candace was the title borne by the queens of the Ethiopians (the kingdom of Cush, in modern Sudan), much as "Pharaoh" was a title of the kings of Egypt; it is named in Scripture in connection with one of the great early conversions of the book of Acts. "And he arose and went: and, behold, a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship" (Acts 8:27). This high official, returning home reading the prophet Isaiah, was met by Philip the evangelist, whom the Spirit had sent to that desert road; Philip, "beginning at the same scripture, preached unto him Jesus" (Acts 8:35), and the eunuch believed and was baptized, going on his way rejoicing. Thus through Candace's treasurer the gospel reached the royal court of an African kingdom in the earliest days of the church. The mention of Candace stands in the dictionary as a marker of the gospel's reach to the ends of the earth, a witness that the risen Christ draws His own from every nation, that the Spirit orchestrates divine appointments to bring one seeking soul to the Savior, and that from the first the good news ran out beyond Israel toward all the peoples of the world.
webster_summary: The dynastic title of the queens of the Ethiopians, named in Acts 8:27; her treasurer, the Ethiopian eunuch, was converted and baptized under Philip, marking the gospel's early reach to the ends of the earth.
webster_full: CANDACE, proper noun. A dynastic title of the queens of the Ethiopians (Cush).
Not a personal name but a royal title, like "Pharaoh."
Her treasurer, a eunuch of great authority, had come to Jerusalem to worship (Acts 8:27).
That eunuch was met by Philip on the desert road and preached Jesus from Isaiah.
He believed, was baptized, and went on his way rejoicing (Acts 8:35-39).

Acts 8:35
Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus.
Acts 8:39

Acts 1:8
...and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
corruption_summary: Candace's mention honors the recovery of the gospel's reach to every nation and the Spirit's sovereign orchestration of conversions, against a narrow view that confines God's saving work to one people or place.
corruption_paragraphs: Narrow-gospel correction. Some imagine the gospel as the possession of one culture or people. The conversion of Candace's treasurer — an African official of a distant court — in the earliest days of the church witnesses to the gospel's reach to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). The dictionary holds that Christ draws His own from every kindred, tongue, people, and nation; the good news was never meant for one people only, but runs out, from the first, toward all the families of the world.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Spirit's sovereign orchestration of divine appointments. God sent Philip from a citywide revival in Samaria to a single seeking soul on a desert road, timing the meeting to the very verse the eunuch was reading. The dictionary commends this providence: the Lord governs every circumstance to bring His chosen ones to the Savior, and no seeking heart, however distant or unlikely, is overlooked by the God who arranges all things to fulfill His saving purpose.
